claim: Hannah Arendt is characterized as the theorist of beginnings whose work, particularly The Human Condition, is highly original and idiosyncratic.
supporting_excerpt: Hannah Arendt is preeminently the theorist of beginnings. All her books are tales of the unexpected (whether concerned with the novel horrors of totalitarianism or the new dawn of revolution), and reflections on the human capacity to start something new pervade her thinking.

claim: Arendt explicitly denied that she intended to propose a blueprint for the future or write political philosophy as conventionally understood.
qualifications: Repudiating the title of political philosopher
supporting_excerpt: But she emphatically denied that her role as a political thinker was to propose a blueprint for the future or to tell anyone what to do. Repudiating the title of “political philosopher,” she argued that the mistake made by all political philosophers since Plato has been to ignore the fundamental condition of politics

claim: The immediate reaction to the launch of the man-made satellite was not triumphal pride, but relief regarding the first step toward escaping human imprisonment to the earth.
supporting_excerpt: The immediate reaction, expressed on the spur of the moment, was relief about the first “step toward escape from men’s imprisonment to the earth.”

claim: The question of whether to use new scientific and technical knowledge to exchange given human existence for something self-made is a political question of the first order rather than a purely scientific one.
qualifications: cannot be decided by scientific means
can hardly be left to the decision of professional scientists or professional politicians alone
supporting_excerpt: The question is only whether we wish to use our new scientific and technical knowledge in this direction, and this question cannot be decided by scientific means; it is a political question of the first order and therefore can hardly be left to the decision of professional scientists or professional politicians.

claim: The term vita activa designates three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action.
supporting_excerpt: With the term vita activa , I propose to designate three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action.

claim: Action corresponds to the human condition of plurality and is specifically the condition of all political life.
supporting_excerpt: Action, the only activity that goes on directly between men without the intermediary of things or matter, corresponds to the human condition of plurality, to the fact that men, not Man, live on the earth and inhabit the world. While all aspects of the human condition are somehow related to politics, this plurality is specifically the condition—not only the conditio sine qua non , but the conditio per quam —of all political life.

claim: Action is the exclusive prerogative of man and is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others, whereas labor and work do not strictly require the company of others in the same way.
supporting_excerpt: Action alone is the exclusive prerogative of man; neither a beast nor a god is capable of it, 1 and only action is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others.

claim: The translation of Aristotle's zōon politikon as animal socialis or homo est naturaliter politicus, id est, socialis reflects a loss of the original Greek understanding of politics.
supporting_excerpt: More than any elaborate theory, this unconscious substitution of the social for the political betrays the extent to which the original Greek understanding of politics had been lost.

claim: The Greek political consciousness clearly and articulately distinguished activities sustaining the life process from the political realm, barring them from entry.
supporting_excerpt: At the root of Greek political consciousness we find an unequaled clarity and articulateness in drawing this distinction. No activity that served only the purpose of making a living, of sustaining only the life process, was permitted to enter the political realm

claim: The emergence of society from the household into the public sphere blurred the boundary between private and political and altered the meaning of both terms.
supporting_excerpt: The emergence of society—the rise of housekeeping, its activities, problems, and organizational devices—from the shadowy interior of the household into the light of the public sphere, has not only blurred the old borderline between private and political, it has also changed almost beyond recognition the meaning of the two terms and their significance for the life of the individual and the citizen.

claim: The law of the ancient city-state was originally identified with the spatial boundary or no man's land between the household and the public realm, serving as a wall that both separated and protected them.
supporting_excerpt: The law originally was identified with this boundary line, 62 which in ancient times was still actually a space, a kind of no man’s land 63 between the private and the public, sheltering and protecting both realms while, at the same time, separating them from each other.

claim: Private wealth became a condition for admission to public life because it assured that its owner was free from the necessity of providing for his own livelihood and could participate in public activity.
supporting_excerpt: Private wealth, therefore, became a condition for admission to public life not because its owner was engaged in accumulating it but, on the contrary, because it assured with reasonable certainty that its owner would not have to engage in providing for himself the means of use and consumption and was free for public activity.

claim: The distinction between labor and work proposed by the author is unusual and lacks substantial precedent in either pre-modern political tradition or modern labor theories.
supporting_excerpt: The distinction between labor and work which I propose is unusual. The phenomenal evidence in its favor is too striking to be ignored, and yet historically it is a fact that apart from a few scattered remarks, which moreover were never developed even in the theories of their authors, there is hardly anything in either the pre-modern tradition of political thought or in the large body of modern labor theories to support it.

claim: Every European language, both ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what has come to be thought of as the same activity.
supporting_excerpt: Against this scarcity of historical evidence, however, stands one very articulate and obstinate testimony, namely, the simple fact that every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what we have to come to think of as the same activity, and retains them in the face of their persistent synonymous usage.

claim: Ancient ancients did not despise labor and work simply because slaves were engaged in them; rather, they felt it necessary to possess slaves because all occupations serving the maintenance of life had a slavish nature.
supporting_excerpt: The opinion that labor and work were despised in antiquity because only slaves were engaged in them is a prejudice of modern historians. The ancients reasoned the other way around and felt it necessary to possess slaves because of the slavish nature of all occupations that served the needs for the maintenance of life.

claim: The institution of slavery in antiquity functioned as an attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man's life rather than as a device for cheap labor or profit-driven exploitation.
supporting_excerpt: The institution of slavery in antiquity, though not in later times, was not a device for cheap labor or an instrument of exploitation for profit but rather the attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man’s life.

claim: Both Smith and Marx shared a contempt for unproductive labor and menial servants who leave nothing behind in return for their consumption.
supporting_excerpt: Moreover, both Smith and Marx were in agreement with modern public opinion when they despised unproductive labor as parasitical, actually a kind of perversion of labor, as though nothing were worthy of this name which did not enrich the world. Marx certainly shared Smith’s contempt for the “menial servants” who like “idle guests . . . leave nothing behind them in return for their consumption.”

claim: Marx's introduction of the term labor power (Arbeitskraft) was considered by Engels to be the most original and revolutionary element of his entire system.
supporting_excerpt: It is because not labor itself but the surplus of human “labor power ” ( Arbeits kraft) explains labor’s productivity that Marx’s introduction of this term, as Engels rightly remarked, constituted the most original and revolutionary element of his whole system.

claim: The distinctions between skilled and unskilled labor and between intellectual and manual work play no role in classical political economy or in Marx's work.
supporting_excerpt: It is interesting to note that the distinctions between skilled and unskilled and between intellectual and manual work play no role in either classical political economy or in Marx’s work.

claim: The distinction between labor and work becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character, location, function, and length of stay of the produced thing are not taken into account.
supporting_excerpt: It seems that the distinction between labor and work, which our theorists have so obstinately neglected and our languages so stubbornly preserved, indeed becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character of the produced thing—its location, function, and length of stay in the world—is not taken into account.

claim: The products of work guarantee the permanence and durability without which a world would not be possible at all, whereas consumer goods are for incessant consumption and lack stability.
supporting_excerpt: Viewed as part of the world, the products of work—and not the products of labor—guarantee the permanence and durability without which a world would not be possible at all.

claim: The least durable tangible things are those needed for the life process itself, which are consumed by use or perish quickly through decay.
supporting_excerpt: The least durable of tangible things are those needed for the life process itself. Their consumption barely survives the act of their production; in the words of Locke, all those “good things” which are “really useful to the life of man,” to the “necessity of subsisting,” are “generally of short duration, such as—if they are not consumed by use—will decay and perish by themselves.”

claim: Laboring always moves in a repetitive circle prescribed by the biological process of the living organism, having no proper beginning or end until the organism dies.
supporting_excerpt: laboring always moves in the same circle, which is prescribed by the biological process of the living organism and the end of its “toil and trouble” comes only with the death of this organism.

claim: Marx defined labor physiologically as man's metabolism with nature, placing labor and consumption as two stages of the biological life cycle.
supporting_excerpt: When Marx defined labor as “man’s metabolism with nature,” in whose process “nature’s material [is] adapted by a change of form to the wants of man,” so that “labour has incorporated itself with its subject,” he indicated clearly that he was “speaking physiologically” and that labor and consumption are but two stages of the ever-recurring cycle of biological life.

claim: Locke, Smith, and Marx each held that labor was the supreme world-building capacity of man, which led them into genuine contradictions due to equating work with labor.
supporting_excerpt: Of the three, however, only Marx was interested in labor as such; Locke was concerned with the institution of private property as the root of society and Smith wished to explain and to secure the unhampered progress of a limitless accumulation of wealth. But all three, though Marx with greatest force and consistency, held that labor was considered to be the supreme world-building capacity of man, and since labor actually is the most natural and least worldly of man’s activities, each of them, and again none more than Marx, found himself in the grip of certain genuine contradictions.

claim: Locke had to introduce money as a lasting thing to allow the laboring body to become the origin of property, because labor naturally produces only things of short duration.
supporting_excerpt: Thus Locke, in order to save labor from its manifest disgrace of producing only “things of short duration,” had to introduce money—a “lasting thing which men may keep without spoiling”—a kind of deus ex machina without which the laboring body, in its obedience to the life process, could never have become the origin of anything so permanent and lasting as property

claim: Marx's thought contains a fundamental contradiction wherein he defines man as an animal laborans while maintaining that human emancipation requires liberation from labor rather than its glorification.
supporting_excerpt: The fact remains that in all stages of his work he defines man as an animal laborans and then leads him into a society in which this greatest and most human power is no longer necessary. We are left with the rather distressing alternative between productive slavery and unproductive freedom.

claim: Locke grounded private property in the body, treating labor as a world-appropriating activity rooted in the ultimate privacy of the human person.
qualifications: applies specifically to Locke's philosophical justification of appropriation
supporting_excerpt: Locke founded private property on the most privately owned thing there is, “the property [of man] in his own person,” that is, in his own body.

claim: Hedonism and the pursuit of an absent of pain represent the most radical forms of a non-political, totally private way of life centered on bodily sensations.
qualifications: linked to consistent sensualism and the historical tradition of Epicurean and Stoic withdrawal
supporting_excerpt: Hedonism, the doctrine that only bodily sensations are real, is but the most radical form of a non-political, totally private way of life, the true fulfilment of Epicurus’ lathe biōsas kai mē politeuesthai (“live in hiding and do not care about the world”).

claim: Pain and the experience of release from pain are uniquely independent from the world because they contain no experience of any worldly object.
supporting_excerpt: In any event, pain and the concomitant experience of release from pain are the only sense experiences that are so independent from the world that they do not contain the experience of any worldly object.

claim: Laboring is the only activity that corresponds strictly to worldlessness or the loss of world found in pain, as the body remains imprisoned in its metabolism with nature.
supporting_excerpt: The only activity which corresponds strictly to the experience of worldlessness, or rather to the loss of world that occurs in pain, is laboring, where the human body, its activity notwithstanding, is also thrown back upon itself, concentrates upon nothing but its own being alive, and remains imprisoned in its metabolism with nature without ever transcending or freeing itself from the recurring cycle of its own functioning.

claim: The concept of process, common to nineteenth-century sciences like economics, history, biology, and geology, was virtually unknown prior to the modern age and became modeled after the biological life process known through introspection, which corresponds to labor.
supporting_excerpt: What all these theories in the various sciences—economics, history, biology, geology—have in common is the concept of process, which was virtually unknown prior to the modern age. Since the discovery of processes by the natural sciences had coincided with the discovery of introspection in philosophy, it is only natural that the biological process within ourselves should eventually become the very model of the new concept; within the framework of experiences given to introspection, we know of no other process but the life process within our bodies, and the only activity into which we can translate it and which corresponds to it is labor.

claim: Neither abundance of goods nor shortened labor time can establish a common world, and an expropriated animal laborans remains private even when deprived of a protective private place, leading to worldless activities like hobbies under socialized conditions.
supporting_excerpt: Neither abundance of goods nor the shortening of the time actually spent in laboring are likely to result in the establishment of a common world, and the expropriated animal laborans becomes no less private because he has been deprived of a private place of his own to hide and be protected from the common realm.

claim: The animal laborans is ejected from the world because of being imprisoned in the privacy of the body and caught in the fulfillment of unshareable and uncommunicable needs.
supporting_excerpt: The animal laborans does not flee the world but is ejected from it in so far as he is imprisoned in the privacy of his own body, caught in the fulfilment of needs in which nobody can share and which nobody can fully communicate.

claim: Pain and effort are the modes in which life and necessity make themselves felt, such that their complete elimination would deprive human life of its liveliness and vitality.
supporting_excerpt: The human condition is such that pain and effort are not just symptoms which can be removed without changing life itself; they are rather the modes in which life itself, together with the necessity to which it is bound, makes itself felt.

claim: Modern improvements in labor tools, such as mute robots, have made the effort of sustaining life and giving birth easier, but they have not eliminated compulsion or human subjection to necessity.
qualifications: has made labor easier and less painful
has not eliminated compulsion or the condition of being subject to need and necessity
supporting_excerpt: It is true that the enormous improvement in our labor tools—the mute robots with which homo faber has come to the help of the animal laborans , as distinguished from the human, speaking instruments (the instrumentum vocale , as the slaves in ancient households were called) whom the man of action had to rule and oppress when he wanted to liberate the animal laborans from its bondage—has made the twofold labor of life, the effort of its sustenance and the pain of giving birth, easier and less painful than it has ever been. This, of course, has not eliminated compulsion from the laboring activity or the condition of being subject to need and necessity from human life.

claim: Tools and instruments are products of work rather than labor, and while they can ease labor and multiply human strength, no work can be produced without tools.
qualifications: not a product of labor but of work
birth of homo faber and the coming into being of a man-made world of things are coeval with the discovery of tools and instruments
supporting_excerpt: Tools and instruments which can ease the effort of labor considerably are themselves not a product of labor but of work; they do not belong in the process of consumption but are part and parcel of the world of use objects. Their role, no matter how great it may be in the labor of any given civilization, can never attain the fundamental importance of tools for all kinds of work. No work can be produced without tools, and the birth of homo faber and the coming into being of a man-made world of things are actually coeval with the discovery of tools and instruments.

claim: Division of labor grows directly out of the laboring process and must be distinguished from the specialization of work.
supporting_excerpt: Division of labor indeed grows directly out of the laboring process and should not be mistaken for the apparently similar principle of specialization which prevails in working processes and with which it is usually equated.

claim: Specialization of work is guided by the finished product requiring different pooled skills, whereas division of labor presupposes qualitative equivalence and exchangeability of activities requiring no special skill.
supporting_excerpt: specialization of work is essentially guided by the finished product itself, whose nature it is to require different skills which then are pooled and organized together, division of labor, on the contrary, presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities for which no special skill is required

claim: The ideals of homo faber, emphasizing permanence and durability, have been sacrificed to the ideal of abundance championed by the animal laborans.
supporting_excerpt: The ideals of homo faber , the fabricator of the world, which are permanence, stability, and durability, have been sacrificed to abundance, the ideal of the animal laborans.

claim: A consumers' society arose not through the political emancipation of the laboring classes, but through the emancipation of the laboring activity itself.
supporting_excerpt: This society did not come about through the emancipation of the laboring classes but by the emancipation of the laboring activity itself, which preceded by centuries the political emancipation of laborers.

claim: All civilizations prior to the modern era viewed the art of earning money as separate from the actual content of other arts and aimed at keeping the worker free from the necessity to labor.
supporting_excerpt: all civilizations prior to our own would rather have agreed with Plato that the “art of earning money” ( technē mistharnētikē ) is entirely unconnected with the actual content even of such arts as medicine, navigation, or architecture, which were attended by monetary rewards.

claim: The modern age's emancipation of labor brought progress toward non-violence, but its status as progress toward freedom is much less certain.
supporting_excerpt: The emancipation of labor and the concomitant emancipation of the laboring classes from oppression and exploitation certainly meant progress in the direction of non-violence. It is much less certain that it was also progress in the direction of freedom.

claim: The danger of future automation lies in human productivity being absorbed into an intensified life process that follows an automatic cycle, wearing down world durability.
supporting_excerpt: The danger of future automation is less the much deplored mechanization and artificialization of natural life than that, its artificiality notwithstanding, all human productivity would be sucked into an enormously intensified life process and would follow automatically, without pain or effort, its ever-recurrent natural cycle.

claim: The spare time of the animal laborans is spent entirely on consumption rather than higher activities, and increased free time only intensifies craving appetites.
supporting_excerpt: the spare time of the animal laborans is never spent in anything but consumption, and the more time left to him, the greedier and more craving his appetites.

claim: The transformation of our economy into a waste economy, where goods are rapidly devoured and discarded, serves as an obvious danger sign indicating we are moving toward the ideal of the animal laborans.
supporting_excerpt: One of the obvious danger signs that we may be on our way to bring into existence the ideal of the animal laborans is the extent to which our whole economy has become a waste economy, in which things must be almost as quickly devoured and discarded as they have appeared in the world, if the process itself is not to come to a sudden catastrophic end.

claim: The human world is composed not of consumed items, but of things that are used, providing the condition under which human life can be at home on earth.
supporting_excerpt: The world, the man-made home erected on earth and made of the material which earthly nature delivers into human hands, consists not of things that are consumed but of things that are used. If nature and the earth generally constitute the condition of human life , then the world and the things of the world constitute the condition under which this specifically human life can be at home on earth.

claim: Fabrication by homo faber involves reification, which inherently entails a violation and destruction of nature by removing materials from their natural locations.
qualifications: applies to fabrication and homo faber
supporting_excerpt: Fabrication, the work of homo faber , consists in reification. Solidity, inherent in all, even the most fragile, things, comes from the material worked upon, but this material itself is not simply given and there, like the fruits of field and trees which we may gather or leave alone without changing the household of nature. Material is already a product of human hands which have removed it from its natural location, either killing a life process, as in the case of the tree which must be destroyed in order to provide wood, or interrupting one of nature’s slower processes, as in the case of iron, stone, or marble torn out of the womb of the earth. This element of violation and violence is present in all fabrication, and homo faber , the creator of the human artifice, has always been a destroyer of nature.

claim: Human productivity modeled after a Creator-God necessarily results in a Promethean revolt because it builds a man-made world by destroying part of God-created nature.
supporting_excerpt: Since his productivity was seen in the image of a Creator-God, so that where God creates ex nihilo , man creates out of given substance, human productivity was by definition bound to result in a Promethean revolt because it could erect a man-made world only after destroying part of God-created nature.

claim: The actual work of fabrication is guided by a model that precedes the process and exists outside the fabricator.
supporting_excerpt: The actual work of fabrication is performed under the guidance of a model in accordance with which the object is constructed. This model can be an image beheld by the eye of the mind or a blueprint in which the image has already found a tentative materialization through work. In either case, what guides the work of fabrication is outside the fabricator and precedes the actual work process

claim: The process of making is entirely determined by the categories of means and end.
supporting_excerpt: The process of making is itself entirely determined by the categories of means and end.

claim: Fabrication is distinguished from all other human activities by having a definite beginning and a predictable end.
supporting_excerpt: To have a definite beginning and a definite, predictable end is the mark of fabrication, which through this characteristic alone dis tinguishes itself from all other human activities.

claim: Homo faber is a master of himself and his doings because he is alone with his image of the future product and free to produce or destroy.
qualifications: True neither of the animal laborans nor of the man of action
supporting_excerpt: Homo faber is indeed a lord and master, not only because he is the master or has set himself up as the master of all nature but because he is master of himself and his doings.

claim: Unlike tools which remain servants of the hand, machines demand that the laborer serve them by adjusting the natural rhythm of the body to mechanical movement.
supporting_excerpt: Unlike the tools of workmanship, which at every given moment in the work process remain the servants of the hand, the machines demand that the laborer serve them, that he adjust the natural rhythm of his body to their mechanical movement.

claim: The first stage of modern technology, marked by the steam engine and industrial revolution, was characterized by the imitation of natural processes and the use of natural forces, powered by newly discovered coal mines.
supporting_excerpt: The first stage, the invention of the steam engine, which led into the industrial revolution, was still characterized by an imitation of natural processes and the use of natural forces for human purposes, which did not differ in principle from the old use of water and wind power.

claim: The channeling of natural forces into the human world has shattered the purposefulness of the world.
supporting_excerpt: The channeling of natural forces into the human world has shattered the very purposefulness of the world, the fact that objects are the ends for which tools and implements are designed.

claim: In automation, the distinction between operation and product, along with the product's precedence over operation, has become obsolete.
supporting_excerpt: In the mode of production ushered in by automation, the distinction between operation and product, as well as the product’s precedence over the operation (which is only the means to produce the end), no longer make sense and have become obsolete.

claim: The continuous automatic process of manufacturing has replaced human standards of utility and beauty with machine-determined product shapes and biological life-process functions.
qualifications: In the context of the continuous automatic process of manufacturing
supporting_excerpt: the continuous automatic process of manufacturing has not only done away with the “unwarranted assumption” that “human hands guided by human brains represent the optimum efficiency,” 15 but with the much more important assumption that the things of the world around us should depend upon human design and be built in accordance with human standards of either utility or beauty.

claim: In the work and fabrication of homo faber, the end justifies the means and organizes the entire work process, but utilitarian ends are perpetually transformed into further means.
qualifications: Relates to homo faber and the activity of fabrication
supporting_excerpt: The implements and tools of homo faber , from which the most fundamental experience of instrumentality arises, determine all work and fabrication. Here it is indeed true that the end justifies the means; it does more, it produces and organizes them.

claim: Consistent utilitarianism suffers from an innate incapacity to distinguish between utility and meaningfulness.
qualifications: Inherent in all consistent utilitarianism
supporting_excerpt: This perplexity, inherent in all consistent utilitarianism, the philosophy of homo faber par excellence, can be diagnosed theoretically as an innate incapacity to understand the distinction between utility and meaningfulness

claim: Establishing utility as meaning generates meaninglessness because it traps thought in an endless chain of means and ends.
supporting_excerpt: The perplexity of utilitarianism is that it gets caught in the unending chain of means and ends without ever arriving at some principle which could justify the category of means and end, that is, of utility itself. The “in order to” has become the content of the “for the sake of”; in other words, utility established as meaning generates meaninglessness.

claim: Homo faber's instrumentalization involves degrading all things into means, leading to a loss of intrinsic and independent value for both manufactured objects and natural forces.
qualifications: In so far as man is homo faber
supporting_excerpt: Man, in so far as he is homo faber , instrumentalizes, and his instrumentalization implies a degradation of all things into means, their loss of intrinsic and independent value, so that eventually not only the objects of fabrication but also “the earth in general and all forces of nature,” which clearly came into being without the help of man and have an existence independent of the human world, lose their “value

claim: The generalization of the fabrication experience turns usefulness and utility into ultimate standards for life and the world, transforming every end into a means.
supporting_excerpt: The issue at stake is, of course, not instrumentality, the use of means to achieve an end, as such, but rather the generalization of the fabrication experience in which usefulness and utility are established as the ultimate standards for life and the world of men.

claim: The modern age aimed to exclude political man (who acts and speaks) from its public realm, much as antiquity sought to exclude homo faber.
qualifications: In both instances the exclusion was not a matter of course
supporting_excerpt: The truth of this remark lies in the fact that the modern age was as intent on excluding political man, that is, man who acts and speaks, from its public realm as antiquity was on excluding homo faber.

claim: Homo faber forms a public realm of his own through the exchange market, driven by the need to show hand-made products and receive esteem.
qualifications: even though it may not be a political realm, properly speaking
supporting_excerpt: His public realm is the exchange market, where he can show the products of his hand and receive the esteem which is due him.

claim: Teamwork is destructive to workmanship because it relies on the division of labor and breaks down operations into constituent motions.
supporting_excerpt: There can be hardly anything more alien or even more destructive to workmanship than teamwork, which actually is only a variety of the division of labor and presupposes the “breakdown of operations into their simple constituent motions.”

claim: The exchange market served historically as the last public realm connected to the activity of homo faber.
supporting_excerpt: Historically, the last public realm, the last meeting place which is at least connected with the activity of homo faber , is the exchange market on which his products are displayed.

claim: Value is exclusively acquired in the public realm through appearance and esteem, distinguishing it from the intrinsic natural worth possessed by a thing in privacy.
supporting_excerpt: Value is the quality a thing can never possess in privacy but acquires automatically the moment it appears in public.

claim: The inherent concept of value entails universal relativity and the loss of intrinsic worth, as things exist only in relation to other things and depend on the fluctuating estimations of supply and demand.
supporting_excerpt: Universal relativity, that a thing exists only in relation to other things, and loss of intrinsic worth, that nothing any longer possesses an “objective” value independent of the ever-changing estimations of supply and demand, are inherent in the very concept of value itself.

claim: Works of art possess supreme durability and distinct uselessness, standing apart from ordinary use objects and exchange markets.
qualifications: applies specifically to works of art within the human artifice
supporting_excerpt: Among the things that give the human artifice the stability without which it could never be a reliable home for men are a number of objects which are strictly without any utility whatsoever and which, moreover, because they are unique, are not exchangeable and therefore defy equalization through a common denominator such as money

claim: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought.
supporting_excerpt: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought, as man’s “propensity to truck and barter” is the source of exchange objects, and as his ability to use is the source of use things.

claim: Art works involve reification as transfiguration, a metamorphosis where thought becomes tangible reality through workmanship.
supporting_excerpt: In the case of art works, reification is more than mere transformation; it is transfiguration, a veritable metamorphosis in which it is as though the course of nature which wills that all fire burn to ashes is reverted and even dust can burst into flames.

claim: Thought and cognition are distinct, with cognition pursuing definite aims and ending when reached, whereas thought has no external end or aim.
supporting_excerpt: Thought and cognition are not the same. Thought, the source of art works, is manifest without transformation or transfiguration in all great philosophy, whereas the chief manifestation of the cognitive processes, by which we acquire and store up knowledge, is the sciences. Cognition always pursues a definite aim, which can be set by practical considerations as well as by “idle curiosity”; but once this aim is reached, the cognitive process has come to an end. Thought, on the contrary, has neither an end nor an aim outside itself, and it does not even produce results

claim: Logical reasoning and intelligence resemble biological labor power and operate through compulsory brain processes akin to the physical laws of nature.
qualifications: applies to intelligence and logical reasoning rather than thought and cognition
supporting_excerpt: In these human faculties we are actually confronted with a sort of brain power which in more than one respect resembles nothing so much as the labor power the human animal develops in its metabolism with nature.

claim: Every manufactured thing transcends pure instrumentality and functional use through its shape, appearing publicly as either beautiful, ugly, or in-between.
qualifications: dependent on having a shape and appearing publicly
supporting_excerpt: By the same token, namely, in its sheer worldly existence, every thing also transcends the sphere of pure instrumentality once it is completed.

claim: The man-made world of things becomes a durable home for mortal men only when it transcends both the functionalism of consumer goods and the sheer utility of objects produced for use.
qualifications: requires transcendence of sheer functionalism and utility to achieve stability
supporting_excerpt: The man-made world of things, the human artifice erected by homo faber , becomes a home for mortal men, whose stability will endure and outlast the ever-changing movement of their lives and actions, only insomuch as it transcends both the sheer functionalism of things produced for consumption and the sheer utility of objects produced for use.

claim: Acting and speaking men require the help of homo faber in his highest capacity, such as artists, poets, and writers, so that the stories they enact and tell can survive.
qualifications: relies on homo faber in his highest capacity
supporting_excerpt: acting and speaking men need the help of homo faber in his highest capacity, that is, the help of the artist, of poets and historiographers, of monument-builders or writers, because without them the only product of their activity, the story they enact and tell, would not survive at all.

claim: Human plurality has a twofold character of equality, which enables understanding and planning across generations, and distinction, which makes speech and action necessary for communication.
supporting_excerpt: Human plurality, the basic condition of both action and speech, has the twofold character of equality and distinction.

claim: Through speech and action, human beings reveal their unique distinctness and appear to each other as persons rather than merely as physical objects.
supporting_excerpt: Speech and action reveal this unique distinctness. Through them, men distinguish themselves instead of being merely distinct; they are the modes in which human beings appear to each other, not indeed as physical objects, but qua men.

claim: The revelatory quality of speech and action emerges in sheer human togetherness where people are neither for nor against each other.
supporting_excerpt: This revelatory quality of speech and action comes to the fore where people are with others and neither for nor against them—that is, in sheer human togetherness.

claim: When action loses the disclosure of the agent and becomes merely a means to an end, it ceases to transcend productive activity.
supporting_excerpt: Without the disclosure of the agent in the act, action loses its specific character and becomes one form of achievement among others.

claim: Human lives tell stories and history becomes the storybook of mankind because both are the outcome of action, resulting in stories with many actors and speakers yet without any tangible authors.
supporting_excerpt: the reason why each human life tells its story and why history ultimately becomes the storybook of mankind, with many actors and speakers and yet without any tangible authors, is that both are the outcome of action.

claim: Plato invented the metaphor of an actor behind the scenes pulling the strings because human affairs and the outcome of action lack a single author, leading him to view human affairs as lacking great seriousness.
supporting_excerpt: Plato, who had no inkling of the modern concept of history, should have been the first to invent the metaphor of an actor behind the scenes who, behind the backs of acting men, pulls the strings and is responsible for the story.

claim: Greek and Latin languages contain two interrelated words for the verb 'to act', reflecting an original division between the initial beginning made by a single person and the subsequent achievement carried out by many.
supporting_excerpt: In order to illustrate what is at stake here we may remember that Greek and Latin, unlike the modern languages, contain two altogether different and yet interrelated words with which to designate the verb “to act.”

claim: Action inherently possesses a boundless quality because every reaction acts as a new independent action that triggers chain reactions, meaning even the smallest act in limited circumstances can change every constellation.
qualifications: applies regardless of the specific content of action
supporting_excerpt: These consequences are boundless, because action, though it may proceed from nowhere, so to speak, acts into a medium where every reaction becomes a chain reaction and where every process is the cause of new processes.

claim: The ancient Greek concept of action was highly individualistic, stressing self-disclosure and serving as the prototype of action and the agonal spirit in city-states.
supporting_excerpt: No doubt this concept of action is highly individualistic, as we would say today. 20 It stresses the urge toward self-disclosure at the expense of all other factors and therefore remains relatively untouched by the predicament of unpredictability. As such it became the prototype of action for Greek antiquity and influenced, in the form of the so-called agonal spirit, the passionate drive to show one’s self in measuring up against others that underlies the concept of politics prevalent in the city-states.

claim: Greeks treated legislation and city-building as prepolitical activities of making (poiēsis) rather than action (praxis), comparing lawmakers to builders and craftsmen.
supporting_excerpt: An outstanding symptom of this prevailing influence is that the Greeks, in distinction from all later developments, did not count legislating among the political activities. In their opinion, the lawmaker was like the builder of the city wall, someone who had to do and finish his work before political activity could begin.

claim: Power is generated and kept alive solely by the living together of people in action and organization, and whoever isolates himself forfeits power.
supporting_excerpt: The only indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people. Only where men live so close together that the potentialities of action are always present can power remain with them, and the foundation of cities, which as city-states have remained paradigmatic for all Western political organization, is therefore indeed the most important material prerequisite for power.

claim: Tyranny rests fundamentally on isolation and contradicts human plurality, thereby generating impotence rather than power.
supporting_excerpt: Montesquieu realized that the outstanding characteristic of tyranny was that it rested on isolation—on the isolation of the tyrant from his subjects and the isolation of the subjects from each other through mutual fear and suspicion—and hence that tyranny was not one form of government among others but contradicted the essential human condition of plurality

claim: The calamities of action arise from human plurality, which is essential for the public realm, making attempts to abolish plurality equivalent to abolishing the public realm.
supporting_excerpt: The calamities of action all arise from the human condition of plurality, which is the condition sine qua non for that space of appearance which is the public realm. Hence the attempt to do away with this plurality is always tantamount to the abolition of the public realm itself.

claim: Political philosophy since Plato can be interpreted as various attempts to escape politics through the concept of rule, which rests on a suspicion of action and a desire to find a substitute for it.
supporting_excerpt: Escape from the frailty of human affairs into the solidity of quiet and order has in fact so much to recommend it that the greater part of political philosophy since Plato could easily be interpreted as various attempts to find theoretical foundations and practical ways for an escape from politics altogether.

claim: The natural sciences have become exclusively sciences of process because the underlying human capacity that brought about this development is the human ability to act and start new unprecedented processes.
supporting_excerpt: The very fact that natural sciences have become exclusively sciences of process and, in their last stage, sciences of potentially irreversible, irremediable “processes of no return” is a clear indication that, whatever the brain power necessary to start them, the actual underlying human capacity which alone could bring about this development is no “theoretical” capacity, neither contemplation nor reason, but the human ability to act—to start new unprecedented processes whose outcome remains uncertain and unpre dictable whether they are let loose in the human or the natural realm.

claim: Men have never been and never will be able to undo or reliably control any of the processes they start through action.
supporting_excerpt: men never have been and never will be able to undo or even to control reliably any of the processes they start through action.

claim: The moral codes inferred from the faculties of forgiving and making promises are entirely based on the presence of others rather than self-relation.
supporting_excerpt: The moral code, on the other hand, inferred from the faculties of forgiving and of making promises, rests on experiences which nobody could ever have with himself, which, on the contrary, are entirely based on the presence of others.

claim: Jesus of Nazareth discovered the role of forgiveness in the realm of human affairs, which holds a strictly secular significance independent of its religious articulation.
qualifications: Articulated in a religious context and language
supporting_excerpt: The discoverer of the role of forgiveness in the realm of human affairs was Jesus of Nazareth. The fact that he made this discovery in a religious context and articulated it in religious language is no reason to take it any less seriously in a strictly secular sense.

claim: The force that keeps people together in public space is mutual promise or contract, which generates a limited reality of sovereignty.
qualifications: applies when many are mutually bound by promises
sovereignty assumes a limited reality
supporting_excerpt: The force that keeps them together, as distinguished from the space of appearances in which they gather and the power which keeps this public space in existence, is the force of mutual promise or contract. Sovereignty, which is always spurious if claimed by an isolated single entity, be it the individual entity of the person or the collective entity of a nation, assumes, in the case of many men mutually bound by promises, a certain limited reality.

claim: Action is the one miracle-working faculty of man that interrupts the automatic, inexorable course of daily life and historical fatality.
qualifications: seen from the viewpoint of automatic processes
supporting_excerpt: Action is, in fact, the one miracle-working faculty of man

claim: Three foundational events determine the character of the modern age: the discovery of America and exploration of the earth, the Reformation and its resulting expropriation and accumulation of social wealth, and the invention of the telescope along with a new universal science.
supporting_excerpt: Three great events stand at the threshold of the modern age and determine its character: the discovery of America and the ensuing exploration of the whole earth; the Reformation, which by expropriating ecclesiastical and monastic possessions started the twofold process of individual expropriation and the accumulation of social wealth; the invention of the telescope and the development of a new science that considers the nature of the earth from the viewpoint of the universe.

claim: Speed has conquered space and rendered distance meaningless by eliminating the necessary time required to reach any point on earth.
qualifications: finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places
supporting_excerpt: Speed has conquered space; and though this conquering process finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places, it has made distance meaningless, for no significant part of a human life—years, months, or even weeks—is any longer necessary to reach any point on the earth.

claim: Galileo's use of the telescope marked an unprecedented event that delivered the secrets of the universe to human cognition with the certainty of sense-perception.
supporting_excerpt: What Galileo did and what nobody had done before was to use the telescope in such a way that the secrets of the universe were delivered to human cognition “with the certainty of sense-perception”

claim: Prior speculations and philosophical hypotheses, such as those of Copernicus and Bruno, lacked the status of an objective historical event until confirmed by empirical facts delivered by the telescope.
qualifications: In the realm of ideas there are only originality and depth, but no absolute, objective novelty
supporting_excerpt: However, neither the speculations of philosophers nor the imaginings of astronomers has ever constituted an event. Prior to the telescopic discoveries of Galileo, Giordano Bruno’s philosophy attracted little attention even among learned men, and without the factual confirmation they bestowed upon the Copernican revolution

claim: Modern philosophy began with Descartes' universal doubt, which replaced the ancient Greek thaumazein (wonder at everything that is) as the central position and motor of thought.
supporting_excerpt: Modern philosophy began with Descartes’ de omnibus dubitandum est , with doubt, but with doubt not as an inherent control of the human mind to guard against deceptions of thought and illusions of sense, not as skepticism against the morals and prejudices of men and times, not even as a critical method in scientific inquiry and philosophic speculation. Cartesian doubt is much more far-reaching in scope and too fundamental in intent to be determined by such concrete contents. In modern philosophy and thought, doubt occupies much the same central position as that occupied for all the centuries before by the Greek thaumazein , the wonder at everything that is as it is.

claim: The most momentous and unavoidable spiritual consequence of modern discoveries has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.
qualifications: follows closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt
supporting_excerpt: Perhaps the most momentous of the spiritual consequences of the discoveries of the modern age and, at the same time, the only one that could not have been avoided, since it followed closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt, has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.

claim: Modern technology originated exclusively in a non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than a pragmatic desire to improve earthly conditions or ease labor.
supporting_excerpt: It is a matter of historical record that modern technology has its origins not in the evolution of those tools man had always devised for the twofold purpose of easing his labors and erecting the human artifice, but exclusively in an altogether non-practical search for useless knowledge.

claim: Homo faber was deprived of permanent measures preceding and outlasting the fabrication process due to the great revolution of modernity.
qualifications: arose from the great revolution of modernity
acquired undreamed-of ingenuity in devising instruments
supporting_excerpt: Homo faber , in other words, as he arose from the great revolution of modernity, though he was to acquire an undreamed-of ingenuity in devising instruments to measure the infinitely large and the infinitely small, was deprived of those permanent measures that precede and outlast the fabrication process and form an authentic and reliable absolute with respect to the fabricating activity.

claim: The principle of utility was superseded by the greatest happiness of the greatest number, reflecting the ultimate failure of homo faber to assert himself.
supporting_excerpt: Nothing perhaps indicates clearer the ultimate failure of homo faber to assert himself than the rapidity with which the principle of utility, the very quintessence of his world view, was found wanting and was superseded by the principle of “the greatest happiness of the greatest number.”

claim: Augustine distinguishes between the question 'Who am I?', directed by man at himself, and 'What am I?', addressed to God.
supporting_excerpt: He distinguishes between the questions of “Who am I?” and “What am I?” the first being directed by man at himself (“And I directed myself at myself and said to me: You, who are you? And I answered: A man”— tu, quis es? [ Confessiones x. 6]) and the second being addressed to God (“What then am I, my God? What is my nature?”— Quid ergo sum, Deus meus? Quae natura sum? [x. 17]).

claim: William L. Westermann argues that Aristotle's statement regarding craftsmen living in limited slavery implies that temporary work contracts forfeit specific elements of free status by volition.
qualifications: Citing William L. Westermann's historical interpretation
supporting_excerpt: William L. Westermann (“Between Slavery and Freedom,” American Historical Review , Vol. L [1945]) holds that the “statement of Aristotle . . . that craftsmen live in a condition of limited slavery meant that the artisan, when he made a work contract, disposed of two of the four elements of his free status [viz., of freedom of economic activity and right of unrestricted movement], but by his own volition and for a temporary period”

claim: In French (ouvrer) and German (werken), as distinguished from modern English usage of labor, the words travailler and arbeiten have largely lost their original connotations of pain and trouble.
supporting_excerpt: This is the case for the French ouvrer and the German werken. In both languages, as distinguished from the current English usage of the word “labor,” the words travailler and arbeiten have almost lost the original significance of pain and trouble

claim: Greek public opinion in the city-states judged occupations based on the effort required and the time consumed.
supporting_excerpt: That Greek public opinion in the city-states judged occupations according to the effort required and the time consumed is supported by a remark of Aristotle about the life of shepherds

claim: Plato introduced the term idea into philosophic terminology, as testified by Aristotle in his Metaphysics.
supporting_excerpt: Aristotle’s testimony that Plato introduced the term idea into philosophic terminology occurs in the first book of his Metaphysics (987b8).

claim: There are labor songs but no work songs, and the songs of craftsmen are social and sung after work.
supporting_excerpt: One of the best of these studies (Joseph Schopp, Das deutsche Arbeitslied [1935]) stresses that there exist only labor songs, but no work songs. The songs of the craftsmen are social; they are sung after work.

claim: The increase in human power over worldly things arises from world alienation, stemming from the distance man places between himself and the world.
supporting_excerpt: The increase in power of man over the things of this world springs in either case from the distance which man puts between himself and the world, that is, from world alienation.

claim: Marx's work remained firmly rooted in the extreme subjectivism of the modern age despite occasional considerations of world alienation.
supporting_excerpt: However, such occasional considerations play a minor role in his work, which remained firmly rooted in the modern age’s extreme subjectivism.

claim: The index entries document various aspects of action, including its definition, properties, and historical or philosophical associations.
supporting_excerpt: action, 175–247 ; the agent as disclosed in, 175–81 ; archein , 177 , 189 , 222–23 , 224 ; in Aristotle’s bios politikos , 12–13 , 25

claim: The index records multiple characteristics and modern figures associated with the concept of animal laborans.
supporting_excerpt: animal laborans: abundance as ideal of, 126 , 134 ; on action and speech as idleness, 208 ; as animal, 84 ; homo faber contrasted with, 136
